hook.text: The only thing connecting your car to the road is four small patches of rubber—about a handprint each.

buildup.text: Tire grip depends on rubber compound, tread pattern, temperature, and road surface.

discovery.text: Soft rubber grips better but wears faster. Hard rubber lasts longer but slips in the cold.

twist.text: A tire slightly slipping—around 10%—actually produces more grip than a fully stuck one.

climax.text: That's why ABS, traction control, and stability systems all manage tiny amounts of wheel slip.

punchline.text: Everything a car does starts at four hand-sized patches.

quiz.question: When does a tire produce maximum grip?

details.summary: Tires are the only part of the car that touches the road, and their rubber compound, tread pattern, and air pressure determine how much grip is available for accelerating, braking, and cornering.
details.whyItMatters: Every safety system depends on tire grip. The best brakes and stability control in the world cannot help if tires lack traction. Proper tire choice and maintenance are critical for safety.
takeaways: The contact patch per tire is roughly the size of a human palm
Tread patterns channel water to prevent hydroplaning
Correct tire pressure maximizes grip, wear life, and fuel economy

faq.question: Do winter tires really make that much difference?
faq.answer: Yes. Winter tires use softer rubber compounds that remain flexible below 45 degrees Fahrenheit and have tread designs that grip snow and ice. They can reduce stopping distances on ice by up to 50 percent.

faq.question: How do I know when my tires need replacing?
faq.answer: When tread depth reaches 2/32 of an inch, the tire is legally worn out. Most tires have built-in wear indicators that become flush with the tread surface at this minimum depth. The penny test also works.
